reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a contract that supposedly automatically buys and sells through PancakeSwap to generate profits, instructing viewers to activate it by transferring BNB and authorizing wallet transactions. It claims potential returns of up to 100 BNB per day and advises adding more funds, despite noting an educational disclaimer and lacking independent verification of the bot's operation or profits.

citations.quote: Today I gonna be deploying a front running bot on PancakeSwap
So we gonna send some funds to the contract we just created.
The action button then will engage with all the constructors I built in and also engaging with the pancake swap router, it automatically buys and sells for you.
We be only competing with other bots and the mempool, and we will automatically sell within 1 min.
we will front run all the retail investors that just come in.

opening.argument: Judge, the profit language should be read alongside the explicit warnings. The description says “FOR EDUCATION PURPOSES ONLY” and “Use at your own risk, not a financial advice.” It also explains why the suggested funding amount matters: “I have received messages from people who didn't have enough funds to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.” That does not prove the bot works, but it is a materially different presentation from a risk-free return promise. The speaker is describing a costly trading experiment, with fees and possible token burns disclosed, rather than claiming that every viewer will profit.

citations.quote: FOR EDUCATION PURPOSES ONLY
Use at your own risk, not a financial advice.
I have received messages from people who didn't have enough funds to cover gas fees and possible burn fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites funding and automated trading, but those steps alone do not establish deception. The description specifically accounts for costs, including “Gas fees average 0.006*2 (0.012 BNB).” Nor does the claimed one-minute sale establish a guaranteed return: the speaker describes when the bot is supposed to sell, not a price at which it must succeed. The warnings deserve weight even if the speaker's enthusiasm is excessive.

citations.quote: Gas fees average 0.006*2 (0.012 BNB).
we will automatically sell within 1 min.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclaimers do not neutralize the pitch. The speaker instructs viewers to fund the contract and activate it, then presents rapid gains as an expected outcome: “Usually it only needs few minutes before profits getting deposit back to our address.” Later, the speaker says viewers “can have upwards 100 BNB per day” and suggests putting more funds into the contract. Fee disclosures do not substantiate those returns or show that the contract performs the claimed trades.

Usually it only needs few minutes before profits getting deposit back to our address
You can run this cycle multiple times a day so you can have upwards 100 BNB per day.
And you can of course put more funds into the initial contract for even make more money.

opening.argument: Judge, the central activity is a software walkthrough. The speaker directs viewers to create a contract file in Remix, inspect token and router addresses, select a compiler version, and deploy using Injected Web3. For example, the speaker says, “just copy and paste on bsc scan for double checking,” then, “So we go to version 6.6. And that's compiled.” The later funding and action steps occur within that same demonstration. Claims about profit should be scrutinized, but the visible workflow and spoken instruction support reading the video as a demonstration of deploying a purported trading bot, not solely as a demand for money.

citations.quote: Under contract I'm creating a new contract. Just hover over this icon and click create new file.
just copy and paste on bsc scan for double checking.
So we go to version 6.6. And that's compiled.
So we gonna do InjectedWeb3. Make sure your wallet is connected to Remix.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats deployment, wallet authorization and funding as proof of a scam, but those are also the operations this walkthrough purports to demonstrate. The speaker describes checking the deployed contract address and says, “For sake of this video – I will do 0.2BNB.” That phrasing makes the transaction part of the example. The cited claims about front-running describe the proposed trading mechanism; they do not, by themselves, establish what the contract actually does.

citations.quote: Now we can adjust copy and paste that contract address to check if it shows up on VSCSCAN.
For sake of this video – I will do 0.2BNB.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can still solicit viewers to fund a purported profit-making contract. Here the speaker tells them to follow the description, download and fund MetaMask, and then models sending funds to the deployed contract. The tutorial culminates in an assertion that the action button automatically buys and sells, followed by claimed gains. The compilation and address-checking steps do not verify the contract's trading behavior or the asserted profits.

citations.quote: So please just follow the description of this video, download MetaMask and also funding it.
So we gonna send some funds to the contract we just created.
The action button then will engage with all the constructors I built in and also engaging with the pancake swap router, it automatically buys and sells for you.
And there we go, we already at around 10x.

opening.argument: Judge, the funding step is real, but its stated destination matters: the speaker says to send funds “to the contract we just created.” The description points viewers to MetaMask, Remix and a smart-contract source, while the speaker describes trading through the PancakeSwap router. On this record, the visible proposition is to operate a trading tool with one's connected wallet; the cited material does not establish that viewers are paying the creator for access, recruiting others for income, or surrendering credentials. Those omissions do not prove the tool is sound, but they weaken the inference that the funding instruction is itself a payment to a scam operator.

also engaging with the pancake swap router, it automatically buys and sells for you.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly notes a BNB transfer and wallet signatures, but neither citation identifies the ultimate beneficiary of the deployed contract. The speaker says viewers can check its address and describes funding “the contract we just created.” The quoted one-minute sale and front-running claims may be implausible; they still do not establish, from the supplied account alone, that a payment goes to the presenter or that the contract cannot trade.

citations.quote: Now we can adjust copy and paste that contract address to check if it shows up on VSCSCAN.
So we gonna send some funds to the contract we just created.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Whether the presenter receives a direct payment is not the only issue. Viewers are told to fund a contract, authorize an action, and expect profits to flow back to their wallets. The speaker then claims a roughly tenfold result and says more initial funding can make more money. The assertion that the address can be checked does not establish what the contract does with deposited BNB, and no cited material independently validates the returns.
